subject: anaesthesia
title: Difficult airway and airway devices: predict to rescue

steps.tx: Prediction starts with the **Mallampati view** of tongue and pharyngeal structures, graded from full visibility to tongue base only. Add the **thyromental distance** of about six centimetres and the **sternomental distance** of about twelve centimetres to judge mandibular space and neck extension. Record dentition, beard, neck mobility, snoring history and prior grades so difficulty never surprises the team.
steps.say: Prediction starts at the mouth and the neck before any drug is given. The Mallampati view is a record of how much pharynx will be seen during laryngoscopy. Thyromental distance is a measure of mandibular space and sternomental distance is a measure of extension. Teeth, beard, neck movement, snoring and prior grades are details that the team shares in one plan.

steps.tx: This image shows four open mouth views that map **Mallampati classes** from full visibility of soft palate and uvula to tongue base only. Progressive loss of fauces and tongue detail marks higher classes with harder **laryngoscopy**. Use the **thyromental distance** alongside the view, because a poor view plus a short mandible warns of difficult intubation and pushes the plan toward awake techniques.
steps.say: Routine induction is a fixed order that is followed every time. Positioning is the opener of the airway and preoxygenation is the builder of reserve for apnoea. Induction with muscle relaxation is the path to gentle mask ventilation followed by laryngoscopy with a bougie that is ready. Capnography is the proof of tracheal placement while bilateral mist is the support. A rescue supraglottic airway is the backup that stays checked and within reach.

vis.alt: Four open mouth views labeled Class I to IV showing progressive loss of visible soft palate, uvula, fauces and tongue base.
vis.caption: Four oral cavity renderings showing Mallampati Class I through IV anatomy. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Routine induction uses sniffing or ramped **positioning**, full **preoxygenation** with apnoeic oxygen flow, and titrated induction with propofol and muscle relaxant. Mask ventilation uses two hands and jaw thrust when needed, then Macintosh or Miller **laryngoscopy** with a bougie ready for first pass success. Confirm placement with capnography and bilateral mist, seat a cuffed tube at the teeth marks, and keep a supraglottic rescue device within reach.
steps.say: This image is a map of Mallampati classes that is asked about every year. The best view is a display of soft palate, uvula and fauces while the worst view is tongue base only. Loss of visible structures is a predictor of harder laryngoscopy with lower first pass rate. The class with thyromental distance and neck mobility is the guide for asleep against awake intubation.

steps.tx: Rescue relies on the **videolaryngoscope** with hyperangulated blade and stylet, awake **fiberoptic intubation** with topicalisation and nerve blocks, and the **supraglottic airway** as an early second seal with gastric drainage. The intubating laryngeal mask acts as a conduit, the Combitube offers dual lumens, jet ventilation temporises, and scalpel bougie tube front of neck access with ECMO backup covers the impossible airway under difficult airway algorithms.
steps.say: Rescue is safe only when the devices are open and assigned. The videolaryngoscope aids viewing around a difficult tongue while the stylet directs the tube, which is key. Awake fiberoptic intubation is the choice for the predicted very difficult airway with topicalisation and blocks. The supraglottic airway restores oxygen when laryngoscopy fails, which is vital. The difficult airway algorithm with early surgical call is the backbone of the plan.

vis.alt: Diagram showing various rescue airway devices: videolaryngoscope, fiberoptic scope, LMA Supreme, iLMA, Combitube, jet transtracheal, and surgical airway.
vis.caption: Key rescue airway devices for difficult intubation

steps.tx: After extubation watch for sore throat, hoarseness, dental or lip **trauma**, aspiration with saturation dips, and **oedema** with stridor that may need nebulised treatment and helium mix. Use staged exchange catheters for risky extubations, arrange anaemia and clinic follow up, and audit first pass success and **capnography** use through registry learning. Never repeat oedematous or bloody attempts blindly, never accept an unrecognised oesophageal trace, and hand over grades with SBAR clarity.
steps.say: Care after the airway is what keeps a good intubation safe. Sore throat and hoarseness are effects that need explanation while dental injury is damage that needs documentation. Aspiration is shown by saturation dips and oedema is shown by stridor after extubation. Risky extubation is staged over an exchange catheter and follow up is arranged. First pass success with handover grade is audited so the unit learns.
